EWI, previously known as Edison Welding Institute, is a nonprofit engineering and technology organization dedicated to developing, testing, and implementing advanced manufacturing technologies for industry. As part this roughly $70M investment, EWI purchased a Sciaky EBAM-110 system in 2016 which can perform both wire-fed additive manufacturing as well as electron beam welding[68]. The EBAM-110 is a 5-axis motion system with low voltage, 42kW internal gun and a 2.7m x 2.7m 2.7m vacuum chamber. Contract research and development with the system included contracts ranging from 1 week to 1 year, including customers in aerospace, defense and nuclear[69]. Marketting of the capability was generally via word of mouth, as well as the EWI mailing list and conference presentations. Initially, the majority of the work concerned additive manufacturing but with time, interest in electron beam welding increased. While utilization of the machine was high during the first years of usage, it is not clear how frequently it is being used at the time of this writing. NASA: Electron beam welding is used extensively during the fabrication of spaceflight hardware. NASA- Marshall in Huntsville, Alabama has utilized a high voltage PTR EBW operated by Aerie Aerospace for research into tungsten joining, with an image of the system shown in Figure 36-left [71]. The ownership structure of this system is unknown and efforts to contact Aerie Aerospace failed. NASA-Langley in Newport News, Virginia operates various electron beam systems, including three small customized research units as well as a commercial Sciaky internal gun systems, shown below. NASA-Langly is the only center that owns and operates an EBW within the agency. NASA-Langley and JLab previously collaborated on the EBW of a 201.25MHz copper cavity for the muon ionization cooling experiment (MICE) [70]. It is important to note that NASA-Langley is a research facility, not a space flight hardware center, and this equipment was originally focused on wire-feed additive manufacturing. When the system was acquired, prior personnel had EBW experience additional skill development was funded over many years of world-leading additive manufacturing(AM) research. This AM R&D was the key to keeping the machine active while moving up the learning curve of both the equipment and process. Use of the machine for AM wanned after an initial surge but interest in wire-feed AM has increased in recent years. Issues regarding the 20 year old control electronics are starting to materialize as the vendor has limited capabilities to support this legacy system.
